Newquay|United Kingdom.f: In 1439 the Bishop of Exeter granted an indulgence to build a new quay, which later gave Newquay its name.

Teesside|United Kingdom.f: In 1979 the largest blast furnace in Europe was erected at the new British Steel plant at Redcar on Teesside.

Bournemouth|United Kingdom.f: Bournemouth grew from 17,000 people in 1880 to 60,000 by 1900 as its railway connections developed.

Humberside|United Kingdom.f: The former county of Humberside stretched from one Wold Newton at its northern tip to another Wold Newton in the south.

Stornoway|United Kingdom.f: Stornoway black pudding was granted protected geographical indication status by the European Commission in 2013.

Exeter|United Kingdom.f: Around AD 55 the Romans founded a 42-acre fort called Isca at the site of Exeter.

Derry|United Kingdom.f: Derry's city walls were built between 1613 and 1619 and remain completely intact, forming a walkway around the inner city.

Norwich|United Kingdom.f: Norwich has returned two members of Parliament since 1298, and was one undivided two-seat constituency until 1950.

Benbecula|United Kingdom.f: In 1746 Bonnie Prince Charlie was caught in a storm and forced to land on Benbecula, before Flora MacDonald smuggled him to Skye.

Wick|United Kingdom.f: Ebenezer Place in Wick is 2.06 metres long with a single door, and is recognised as the world's shortest street.

Islay|United Kingdom.f: Islay has nine active whisky distilleries, down from as many as 23 at one time.

Kirkwall|United Kingdom.f: Kirkwall was first mentioned in the Orkneyinga saga in 1046, as the home of Rognvald Brusason.

Campbeltown|United Kingdom.f: Campbeltown once had over 30 distilleries and proclaimed itself the whisky capital of the world.

Tiree|United Kingdom.f: Tiree holds the Scottish record for sunshine in a single month, with 329.1 hours in May 1975.

Dundee|United Kingdom.f: At its height Dundee supported 62 jute mills employing some 50,000 workers.

Eday|United Kingdom.f: Eday hosts a European Marine Energy Centre tidal test site where currents reach almost 4 m/s at spring tides.

Oban|United Kingdom.f: Work on Oban's McCaig's Tower began in 1895 and stopped in 1902 on the death of its benefactor.

Land's End|United Kingdom.f: The road from Land's End to John o' Groats in Scotland is 838 miles long, a route often used for charity challenges.

Fair Isle|United Kingdom.f: The Spanish Armada flagship El Gran Grifon was wrecked on Fair Isle in 1588, and its 300 sailors lived with islanders for six weeks.

North Ronaldsay|United Kingdom.f: North Ronaldsay's rare sheep feed mostly on seaweed, and a 1.8 m dry stone dyke rings the island to keep them off farmland.

Papa Westray|United Kingdom.f: Papa Westray's Knap of Howar farmstead, dating from around 3500 BC, is the oldest preserved house in northern Europe.

Westray|United Kingdom.f: The Westray Wife, a 4 cm Neolithic figurine found in 2009, is the oldest carving of a human found in the British Isles.

Stronsay|United Kingdom.f: In 1913 the Fishery Board for Scotland called Stronsay the principal herring curing station in the Orkney district.

Colonsay|United Kingdom.f: Colonsay is the smallest island in the world with its own brewery.

Coll|United Kingdom.f: Coll gained dark skies status in December 2013, the second location in Scotland to do so.

Sanday|United Kingdom.f: Sanday takes its name from Old Norse Sandey, meaning sand island, because of its many sandy beaches.

Foula|United Kingdom.f: Foula's western cliffs plunge 150 to 365 metres, and the island starred in the 1937 film The Edge of the World.
